title: AI & Your Money
hook: AI is a great explainer of money and a decent budgeting helper — but a risky advisor. Use it to understand your finances, not to make the calls or to hand over your account details.
key_points: Excellent for plain-English explanations: what's an ETF, how does APR work, what's a Roth IRA.
Handy for budgeting drafts, comparison questions, and prepping to talk to a professional.
Don't trust it for specific numbers, tax/legal advice, or 'what should I buy' calls.
Never hand it bank logins, card numbers, or account access — and beware AI investment scams.
content_html: Money is one of the areas where AI is both genuinely useful and genuinely risky, and the line between the two is worth getting right. On the useful side, a chatbot is a wonderful, judgment-free financial explainer. You can ask what an index fund is, how credit card interest actually compounds, what the difference is between gross and net, or what a term in your insurance policy means — and get a clear, patient answer at whatever level you need. It's also handy for the scaffolding of money management: drafting a monthly budget from your numbers, listing questions to ask a mortgage broker, or comparing the general pros and cons of two approaches before you talk to a real professional.
extra_html: The risky side is just as important. AI should not be your financial advisor. It can state specific figures, tax rules, or "best" products with total confidence and be wrong, and it knows nothing about your actual situation, risk tolerance, or local laws. Treat any concrete number, tax claim, or "you should buy X" as unverified — confirm it with official sources or a qualified human before acting, especially where real money or the tax authorities are involved. Two hard rules keep you safe: never give an AI tool (or a website pretending to be one) your bank logins, card numbers, or account access; and be deeply skeptical of "AI-powered" investment or trading schemes, which have become a favorite scam dressed up with fake celebrity endorsements and promises of guaranteed returns. Use AI to understand your money better — then make the decisions yourself, with real advice where it counts.

related.title: AI Scams & Staying Safe
related.hook: AI didn't invent scams — it just made them cheaper, faster, and far more convincing. The good news: the habits that beat them haven't changed.

related.title: When AI Makes Things Up
related.hook: AI 'hallucinations' aren't glitches — they're the technology working as designed. A model that always predicts a plausible next word will sometimes produce a plausible falsehood.

related.title: Your Data & Privacy
related.hook: When you type into a free AI tool, you might be the product. What you share can be stored, reviewed by humans, and used to train future models — so share like it's not private.

flashcards.prompt: What's a good use of AI for personal finance?

choices.text: Explaining financial concepts in plain language and drafting a budget
Picking exactly which stocks to buy with your savings
Logging into your bank to manage your money

flashcards.explanation_html: AI shines at explaining concepts and organizing a budget. It's unreliable for specific advice and should never be given account access.

flashcards.prompt: Why be cautious about 'AI investment' opportunities advertised online?
flashcards.back_html: Many are scams — using AI branding, fake testimonials, or deepfakes of celebrities to lend false credibility. Treat them like any too-good-to-be-true pitch.
